# `js/id-denylist`

**No identifier the project denies**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Pack** | `@codelaw/rules-js` (npm) · `codelaw-rules-js` (PyPI) |
| **Languages** | JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, TSX |
| **Turned on by** | no preset — name it in `[rules]` |
| **Severity when named without one** | `error` |
| **Options** | `names` |
| **Fix** | `manual` — no automatic fix; the steps are under *How to fix* (the name to use instead is the author's) |
| **Stability** | `preview` — runs only with `preview = true` |
| **Since** | 0.5.2 |
| **Ported from** | `eslint/id-denylist` |

## What it checks

An identifier named in `names` is reported wherever the file declares, assigns or reads it: `names = ["data", "temp", "e"]` flags `const data`, `function f(temp)` and `catch (e)`. Behaviour of ESLint 10.13.0's `id-denylist`, read and reimplemented. As upstream, these are not checked: a name that is directly a call's callee or argument (`use(data)`), a property read (`item.data`, but `item.data = 1` is), the old name in `import { data as records }` and a destructuring key (`const { data: records } = source`), and a reference to a global the file does not declare.

Set the option to switch it on, for example `[rules] "js/id-denylist" = { severity = "error", options = { names = ["data", "temp", "e"] } }`. With no `names` set the rule is silent: it reports nothing, not even that the option is missing, and the engine does not run it on a single node. It is in no preset; a project switches it on by setting the option under `[rules]` (or in a `[scope.<name>]` for some files).

**Why:** A project denies names that say nothing (`data`, `temp`, `e`) so that each name tells the reader what the value is.

## Configuration

Everything below goes in `codelaw.toml` at the repo root. The same keys work as `[tool.codelaw]` in `pyproject.toml` or `"codelaw"` in `package.json` ([SR-CONFIG](../../../records/0110_config.md)).

### Turn it on

**Install the pack** (`codelaw init` does it for the languages it finds):

```bash
npm install --save-dev @codelaw/rules-js
pip install codelaw-rules-js
```

**No preset turns it on.** Load its pack through any preset (`codelaw:js/recommended` here), then name the rule in `[rules]`:

```toml
preview = true                        # pack rules are preview today
extends = ["codelaw:js/recommended"]

[rules]
"js/id-denylist" = "error"
```

- **A rule exists only once its pack is loaded** through `extends`; naming it in `[rules]` without that is an unknown rule id (exit 2).
- **Without `preview = true`** the rule is skipped and codelaw warns that it is preview.

### Severity

```toml
[rules]
"js/id-denylist" = "warn"    # error | warn | info | off
```

- **`error`** fails the run (exit 1) · **`warn`** fails only with `--max-warnings N` · **`info`** never fails · **`off`** turns it off.
- **Naming it with a severity turns it on** even when no preset does.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `names` | `string[]` | `[]` | identifier names that may not be used |

**Every option at its default** — a starting point to copy:

```toml
[rules."js/id-denylist"]
severity = "error"

[rules."js/id-denylist".options]
names = []
```

**The same, inline, with example values:**

```toml
[rules]
"js/id-denylist" = { severity = "error", options = { names = ["data", "temp", "e"] } }
```

- **A table without `severity`** changes only the options: the severity stays what a preset or an earlier layer set, and a rule that is off stays off.
- **A list option replaces its default** — copy the default entries you want to keep.
- **An unknown option or a value of the wrong type** stops the run with exit 2 and names the nearest option.

#### `names`

*string[]* · default `[]`

identifier names that may not be used

```toml
[rules."js/id-denylist".options]
names = ["data", "temp", "e"]
```

### Options in action

Each case below is one of the rule's tests (`packs/js/rules/js/id-denylist.cases.md`): the options, the input, and what codelaw reports.

#### a declaration, a parameter and a catch clause

```toml
[rules."js/id-denylist".options]
names = ["data", "temp", "e"]
```

```js
const data = load();
function run(temp) {
  return temp;
}
try {
  run(data);
} catch (e) {
  throw e;
}
```

**Reports** at `1:7`, `2:14`, `3:10`, `7:10`, `8:9`.

#### a call's callee and arguments are not checked

```toml
[rules."js/id-denylist".options]
names = ["data"]
```

```js
const result = format(data);
const again = data(1);
```

**Reports nothing.**

#### a property is checked when it is assigned to

```toml
[rules."js/id-denylist".options]
names = ["data"]
```

```js
item.data = 1;
const x = item.data;
```

**Reports** at `1:6`.

#### a global the file does not declare

```toml
[rules."js/id-denylist".options]
names = ["data"]
```

```js
const copy = data;
```

**Reports nothing.**

#### an object key

```toml
[rules."js/id-denylist".options]
names = ["data"]
```

```js
const options = { data: 1 };
```

**Reports** at `1:19`.

#### a destructuring key and a renamed import are the other name's

```toml
[rules."js/id-denylist".options]
names = ["data"]
```

```js
const { data: records } = source;
import { data as items } from "./store";
```

**Reports nothing.**

#### a private name

```toml
[rules."js/id-denylist".options]
names = ["data"]
```

```js
class Store {
  #data = 1;
}
```

**Reports** at `2:3`.

### For a group of files

A `[scope.<name>]` gives some files their own setting, applied after `[rules]` — the `tests` scope `codelaw:js/recommended` ships (`**/*.test.*`, `**/*.spec.*`); naming it extends it, so its files stay:

```toml
[scope.tests]
rules = { "js/id-denylist" = { options = { names = ["data", "temp", "e"] } } }
```

Or switch it off there:

```toml
[scope.tests]
rules = { "js/id-denylist" = "off" }
```

A scope's `remap` changes whole severities in its files, after everything else: `remap = { error = "warn" }` never fails the run there.

### Warn locally, fail in CI

The `ci` profile runs when `CI` is set; `local` otherwise; `--profile <name>` or `CODELAW_PROFILE` picks one.

```toml
[profile.local.rules]
"js/id-denylist" = "warn"

[profile.ci.rules]
"js/id-denylist" = "error"
```

### In `pyproject.toml` or `package.json`

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[tool.codelaw.rules]
"js/id-denylist" = { severity = "warn", options = { names = ["data", "temp", "e"] } }
```

```json
{
  "codelaw": {
    "rules": {
      "js/id-denylist": {"severity": "warn", "options": {"names": ["data", "temp", "e"]}}
    }
  }
}
```

### Silence one finding

An inline `codelaw-ignore` always needs a reason; `expires=`, `warn_days=` and `by=` date it ([SR-LINTER](../../../records/0106_linter.md) decision 6).

- **JavaScript:** `// codelaw-ignore js/id-denylist: <reason>`
- **Dated:** `// codelaw-ignore js/id-denylist expires=2026-12-31 by=you@example.com: <reason>`

### Keep today's findings, fail on new ones

```bash
codelaw baseline add --rule js/id-denylist --expires 2026-12-31 --reason "<why>"
```

See [SR-BASELINE](../../../records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md).

### See what applies

```bash
codelaw explain js/id-denylist       # what it wants, why, how to fix
codelaw check --rule js/id-denylist  # only this rule
codelaw config --print --for <file>  # the resolved setting, and where it came from
```

## How to fix

1. Rename it to a name that says what it holds, in the declaration and every use.

## Examples

### JavaScript

#### Don't

*With these options:* `{ names = ["data", "temp", "e"] }`

```js
const data = load();
```

#### Do

*With these options:* `{ names = ["data", "temp", "e"] }`

```js
const records = load();
```

### JSX

#### Don't

*With these options:* `{ names = ["data", "temp", "e"] }`

```jsx
const data = load();
```

#### Do

*With these options:* `{ names = ["data", "temp", "e"] }`

```jsx
const records = load();
```
